name: GLM-5.2 API — a frontier coding model on your six GPUs, driven from your own machine
description: The model, published as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with nothing else in the container. Your agent stays on your laptop — opencode, Cline, Roo Code, aider, Continue — and keeps working on your real repository, with your git remotes, your dotfiles and your uncommitted branch; only prompts and diffs cross the wire. This is the variant to pick when the code already lives on your machine. Its sibling glm52-opencode runs the agent inside the container instead, which is the better answer for a greenfield or git-backed project and the wrong one for a working tree you already have. GLM-5.2 is a 744-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model activating about 40 billion parameters per token, which is how a model this large answers at a usable speed: 62.1 on SWE-bench Pro and 81.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, the strongest openly published coding scores available, with a 131K-token context here. WHAT MAKES IT USABLE BY AN AGENT rather than just a chat client: vLLM is started with the glm47 tool parser, --enable-auto-tool-choice and the glm45 reasoning parser. Those three flags are the entire difference between an endpoint an agent can drive and one it cannot. Without the first two the server answers HTTP 400 to tool_choice:"auto", which is every request opencode and Cline send, so the agent fails before reading a single file. Without the third, GLM's thinking block is returned as ordinary content with the tool call still buried inside it, so the client sees a chatty assistant that never calls anything. The launch script proves both by sending itself a real tool-calling request before the service is published. ONE REQUIREMENT AT LAUNCH, enforced by the startup script rather than discovered later: set VLLM_API_KEY, 24 characters or more, generated rather than chosen. This template publishes the inference API itself, the node binds container ports straight to the host with no auth layer in front of them, and vLLM's --api-key is the only access control in the entire path. An unset key means a frontier model on a public IP for the whole escrow window, and because --max-num-seqs is 8, a leaked key does not merely steal tokens — it starves you off your own box. Two things follow, and neither is theoretical: the endpoint is plain http, so the key and every prompt travel in cleartext and belong behind a TLS-terminating proxy or a VPN before they carry anything that matters; and the key should be rotated by relaunching rather than shared. ALSO SELECT A PERSISTENT-STORAGE BUCKET. It holds the 753 GB of weights plus the torch.compile and Triton caches, and the node builds a fresh container on every launch, so without one the weights re-download inside your paid window and every kernel recompiles on six workers. The container refuses to start rather than let that happen. FIRST LAUNCH IS SLOW AND THAT TIME IS BILLED: the weights are fetched from Hugging Face before the model can load, roughly one and a half to two hours on a gigabit link. Set HF_TOKEN to avoid anonymous rate limits across 141 shards. Every launch after that reads from your bucket and starts in minutes. Buy a duration that accounts for the first one, and keep using the same bucket. The service is not published until the script has sent it a real request and a real tool call and got answers back, so a container reporting Running can actually serve — pipeline-parallel models allocate memory on the first request that startup cannot see, and discovering that by typing a prompt is how a paid window gets wasted. CLIENT CONFIG: base URL http://<host>:<port>/v1, bearer token the key you set, model id glm-5.2, context 131072. REQUIREMENTS THIS TEMPLATE WILL NOT COMPROMISE ON, each checked before the download starts so a mistake costs seconds rather than hours: VLLM_API_KEY, a mounted bucket, exactly six GPUs of the 141 GB H200 class (132 GB is the arithmetic floor), a large /dev/shm (the node operator must configure it — see the GPU note below), and around 800 GB free on the bucket. If any is missing the container exits immediately with a log line saying which.
outcome: Run your own agent on your own files against a frontier-class 744B coding model hosted entirely on your six GPUs — no code leaves your machine, and the weights persist across launches.

workflows.name: Weights and compile-cache bucket
workflows.description: Not a workflow. This entry exists so the launch wizard offers the bucket picker: nodes-dashboard gates that picker on workflows[].length > 0 (templateNeedsBucketPicker in src/services/template-launch.ts). The bucket holds the 753 GB of model weights and the torch.compile/Triton caches — without it the container refuses to start. The graph is deliberately empty and the container ignores COMFY_WORKFLOW entirely. Delete this once the node exposes a declarative persistence field.

requiredResources.description: EXACTLY six CUDA GPUs of at least 132 GB VRAM each — in practice the 141 GB H200 class — on one host, ideally NVLink-connected. Six is not a suggestion and not a minimum to round up from: the model is 753 GB in FP8 and is split with tensor-parallel size 2 across pipeline-parallel size 3, which is the only layout that fits. Tensor-parallel 6 is arithmetically impossible here (64 attention heads, which 6 does not divide, and neither does 3), and replicating the model per GPU would need 140 GB of a 141 GB card before any cache. At this layout each card holds about 125.5 GB of weights, which is why 132 GB is a floor and not a preference: six 96 GB cards cannot run this and never could, 576 GB of VRAM against 753 GB of weights. Note that a 141 GB card is 131.3 GiB, not 141 GiB — the difference is larger than the whole KV cache budget, and mistaking one for the other is how a launch fails at the KV allocation step with 0.94 GiB available. vLLM is given 95% of the card rather than everything that fits, because a pipeline-parallel model allocates memory on its FIRST REQUEST that startup never profiles: the per-stage NCCL communicators are created lazily on the first hidden-state send, at roughly 100 MB each, alongside the sparse-prefill workspace and a kernel that JIT-compiles mid-inference. Squeeze that headroom out and the service loads, reports healthy, then dies on the first prompt with an NCCL out-of-memory error from irecv_tensor_dict. The squeeze at the other end is the pipeline split, and it is why the context here is 131072 rather than the model's full 262144. The three stages hold 26 layers each, which is even in layers and badly uneven in bytes: measured on 6x141 GB, stage 0 finishes with 16.81 GiB free for KV cache while the tightest stage has 1.87 GiB, and since pipeline parallelism needs a uniform page count across stages, the smallest one sets the pool and ~14.9 GiB of stage 0 goes unused. The last stage also carries the LM head, and its CUDA graph capture costs 2.2-2.4 GiB against 0.64 GiB in the middle (graph memory sits inside the utilisation budget since vLLM 0.21.0). To recover the full context on this hardware, balance the stages rather than raising utilisation: launch once, read the per-stage 'Available KV cache memory' lines from the log, and redistribute with VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION — the stranded 14.9 GiB is more than 262144 needs. VLLM_GPU_MEM_UTIL, VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN and VLLM_MAX_NUM_SEQS are all overridable for larger cards. The launch script proves the whole configuration by serving itself a real request AND a real tool call before the service is published, so a wrong value costs seconds instead of a paid window. ONE OPERATOR PREREQUISITE: a service spanning several GPUs runs one worker process per card, and those processes exchange data through shared memory, so the node must give this container more than Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm. The node operator sets this once per GPU resource via init.advanced (ShmSize, optionally IpcMode, PidsLimit) — see docs/compute.md, 'Multi-GPU workloads'. The launch script checks for it up front and exits with an explanatory log line rather than failing obscurely deep inside model loading. Nothing else in this container competes for VRAM: there is no UI, no embedding model and no agent process, only vLLM.
